title: Making Quantum Networks Work: Routing, Calibration, and Programmable Quantum Repeaters
abstract: The quantum internet enables distribution of quantum states across distant nodes, supporting secure communication, distributed computing, and quantum sensing. Unlike classical networks, it is constrained by the no cloning theorem, probabilistic entanglement generation, decoherence, and hardware drift, making classical abstractions inadequate. Scalable quantum networking therefore requires new architectures, protocols, and optimisation methods that explicitly account for these limitations.   This thesis studies the architecture, routing, and operation of quantum networks under realistic constraints, focusing on bipartite entanglement distribution over quantum repeater networks. Key metrics include end to end fidelity, throughput, scalability, and fairness. At the network layer, routing strategies are developed beyond assumptions of homogeneous nodes and full network knowledge. Routing under heterogeneous repeater efficiencies shows how partial knowledge of node quality improves fidelity and reduces path blocking. A grey box routing approach is then introduced, where path selection relies only on topology and end to end estimates, achieving robustness and fairness without detailed link information.   At the link layer, calibration and hardware drift are addressed through a calibration aware model separating activation and calibration phases. For linear repeater chains, an optimal calibration schedule is derived to balance operation time and calibration overhead. This is extended to general topologies with shared links, where a greedy orchestration heuristic is proposed.   Finally, the thesis connects network protocols with hardware via an instruction set architecture for programmable quantum repeater nodes based on NV centers, enabling coherent programmability and linking physical operations to higher layer protocols.
summary: This thesis addresses the complexity of building scalable quantum networks by integrating three previously separate domains: routing, link calibration, and hardware programmability. It develops a cross-layer framework that allows protocols to function reliably even with partial knowledge of imperfect physical links. The result is a comprehensive model for programmable quantum repeaters necessary for long-distance quantum communication.
main_problem: The core challenge is designing scalable quantum networks by developing integrated protocols for routing, managing link imperfections via calibration, and implementing programmable hardware at the repeater nodes.
main_result: The thesis proposes a cross-layer framework where grey-box routing achieves robustness using partial knowledge, while explicit calibration schedules and an Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) enable reliable operation despite hardware drift.
method: The work combines theoretical protocol development with architectural modeling, deriving optimal scheduling algorithms for link calibration and proposing a concrete ISA interface for physical quantum repeaters.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum network designed for long-distance entanglement distribution. It models components like qubits (e.g., NV centers), entanglement swapping operations, and the interaction between network protocols and underlying hardware control layers.
key_observables: End to end fidelity ($\mathcal{F}_{	ext{ete}}$), Blocking Probability (BP), Throughput ($T$), and operational efficiency metrics.
important_parameters: Link fidelity decay rate ($\Gamma_e$), calibration overhead time, network topology parameters, and the size/capability of the programmable node register.
main_assumptions: The research moves beyond assuming full or static knowledge of link properties, instead modeling partial knowledge and dynamic hardware limitations as fundamental constraints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate entanglement generation schemes (MeetInTheMiddle, Sender-Receiver), network topologies (Grid/Cylindrical), and performance comparisons showing how BP and Fidelity vary with node quality ($\xi$) under different routing algorithms.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for a cross-layer view; it then details routing strategies using grey-box approaches, followed by developing calibration-aware models for link operation, culminating in the proposal of an ISA for programmable repeater nodes.
why_interesting: It provides a comprehensive blueprint for realizing quantum internet infrastructure by explicitly linking high-level network protocols (routing) to low-level physical control mechanisms (ISA/calibration), which is crucial for experimental realization using solid-state qubits.
